title: Just had a crazy breakthrough idea for generating sprites
author: sjun0608
selftext:
Model a dummy character in Blender, rig it, make animations for different actions, and capture them frame by frame. Then ask for the dummy sprites along with the prompts

Then feed those sprites and prompts into chatgpt alongside the target character's image using Image 2.5 to generate the sprites- feels like it'd give pretty usable results?

Of course I hit my Codex limit, so I haven't been able to test it yet

comments.author: Grijpstuivert
comments.body: Yeah, I tried this with 5.6 sol. Modeled it after the Factorio workflow (they have a lot of documentation on their website) It kind of works, but it leaves more and more room for error the more animations you have. It gives you an increasingly big list of sprites that each individually can contain errors, especially if you let it generate more than 1 direction in 1 image. I ended up ditching the idea because making all the different sprites took a really long time and fixing the I evitable bugs took me even longer. When I finally had a decent character I realised I would have to do this for many more assets. When you have a 3d model at least that is the one thing you have to check. With the improvement astra made in making 3d models I don't think it's worth the hassle of generating all the different sprites and trying to get them to work with the animations.

replies.author: FailedGradAdmissions
replies.body:
Not the best, but I find it much more productive to just have a 2D pixel shaders on top of a 3d model. Looks decent and lots of indie games go that way so it's a proven method.

And as a bonus it makes accurate shadows trivial.

comments.author: keradius
comments.body: I did try this technique before, not all image generation takes skeletons as input, also the results are variable depending on angle, side performa ok, top down pretty terribly

comments.author: Charming_You_25
comments.body:
Yes I tried this, issue is you need to send them 1 by 1 if you need 100% accuracy. You can do rows as long as they are the same direction. The trick is they also need to be lined up in the direction they are moving, so you can’t have a 45 degree view in a row. You have to generate them so they are walking in a 45 degree angle across the screen, which leaves a lot of wasted space and adds complexity separating the frames.

Anytime you have more than 1 the image model can get confused.

comments.body: Sounds similar to the manual technique of "rotoscoping".  Maybe you can try asking ai to apply rotoscoping to your blender animation to see what happens.  Sounds like a great way to make realistic sprites.

comments.author: reality_comes
comments.body:
Here is how i do it. 

Generate an image of a character you like in a neutral pose facing forward.

Pass that to a video model like grok imagine or a local model and prompt the character to do the action you want.

Save the frames you need for the animation. 

I had codex build a tool to assemble the images into sheets with set rows for the actions. 

You can take a neutral version of this sheet with maybe 2 rows at a time or 3 and give it to a good image model and provide it with a new character to copy the animation to. 

Slowest part is picking the frames you want.
